Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, let $n\ge1$, and let $1\le k\le n$ be an integer. Given $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in H^n$, put $q=\lfloor n/k\rfloor$ and $r=n-kq$. Form consecutive blocks $B_1,\ldots,B_k$ in index order, with $|B_j|=q+1$ for $j\le r$ and $|B_j|=q$ for $j>r$. Compute the block means $m_j=|B_j|^{-1}\sum_{i\in B_j}x_i$. Return the unique minimum-norm point of
$$
\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in H}\sum_{j=1}^k\|z-m_j\|.
$$

The objective minimizers are called geometric medians of the block means. The minimum-norm rule makes the output single-valued. Existence, uniqueness of that selected point, and Borel measurability as a function of the input tuple are proved in [[lem-measurable-minimum-norm-geometric-median-selection]].

Let $\mathcal Z=\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y$ be a feature-response measurable
space, let $m\ge0$, and put $n=m+1$. A **split score rule** is a jointly
measurable map $s:\mathcal H\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R$, where $H$ is a
training statistic with values in the specified measurable rule space
$(\mathcal H,\mathscr H)$. The measurable-statistic convention is that of
[[def-statistic-and-estimator]]. Once $H=h$ is fixed, calibration and test
scores are $R_i=s(h,Z_i)$; the rule does not change when it scores the
calibration or test example.

A **full score assignment** of length $n$ is a measurable map
$A=(A_1,\ldots,A_n):\mathcal Z^n\to\mathbb R^n$ that is
permutation-equivariant:
$$A(\tau_\pi z)=\tau_\pi A(z)\qquad\text{for every }z\in\mathcal Z^n\text{ and permutation }\pi.$$
For a candidate response $y$, append $(x,y)$ as the $n$th example and write
$R_i(y)=A_i(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m,(x,y))$ and $r=R_n(y)$.

For either a split score vector or a full augmented score vector, the
**nonrandomized upper-rank p-value** of the candidate is
$$p(y)=\frac1{m+1}\sum_{i=1}^{m+1}\mathbf1\{R_i(y)\ge R_{m+1}(y)\}.$$
An optional **tie-randomized rank p-value** is defined when a supplied random
variable $U$ has Lebesgue probability law on $[0,1]$ and is independent of the
data and training information:
$$p_U(y)=\frac{\#\{i\le m:R_i(y)>r\}+U\bigl(1+\#\{i\le m:R_i(y)=r\}\bigr)}{m+1}.$$
The added $1$ counts the candidate itself in its tie group. A single such $U$
is shared across a candidate scan. This is an explicit randomization; the
general Markov-kernel definition of a randomized procedure
[[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]] does not assert that arbitrary
kernels have a random-seed representation.

Here “uniform on $[0,1]$” means $\mathbb P(U\le u)=u$ for $0\le u\le1$.

Smaller scores are treated as more conforming. The rank formula counts all
ties conservatively in the nonrandomized version; the randomized formula
spreads the candidate uniformly over its entire tie block.

Let $\mathcal B$ be the Borel sigma-algebra of $[0,1]$, generated by intervals with rational endpoints; let $dt$ be Lebesgue measure restricted to $\mathcal B$, and set $H=L^2([0,1],\mathcal B,dt;\mathbb R)$, with inner product $\langle x,y\rangle_H=\int_0^1x(u)y(u)\,du$. We use the quotient-by-null-functions convention for $L^2$ ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). The measure space is finite and countably generated, so under Countable Choice $H$ is separable ([[thm-l-p-of-a-sigma-finite-countably-generated-measure-space-is-separable]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-separable-space]]); [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]] verifies that this real pairing makes the quotient a Hilbert space.

Let $(S,\mathcal S,\nu)$ be a probability space and $(\delta_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ an independent identically distributed family of $S$-valued random elements with law $\nu$ ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]], [[def-independent-random-elements]]). A **causal Bernoulli shift** with innovation law $\nu$ is a process
$$X_t=f(\delta_t,\delta_{t-1},\delta_{t-2},\ldots),\qquad t\in\mathbb Z,$$
where $f:S^{\mathbb N_0}\to H$ is measurable from the product sigma-algebra $\mathcal S^{\otimes\mathbb N_0}$ to the Borel sigma-algebra of $H$. This product-measurability formulation is meaningful for a merely measurable innovation space $S$.

On an independent product extension, take replacement innovations $\delta'_{t,m,k}$, indexed by $t\in\mathbb Z$, $m\in\mathbb N_0$, and integers $k\le t-m$, all with law $\nu$, mutually independent, and independent of the original innovations. Such a countable family and its product with the original probability space exist under Countable Choice and Dependent Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-dependent-choice]], [[cor-countable-independent-copies-exist]], [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]). For $m\ge1$ define
$$X_{t,m}=f(\delta_t,\ldots,\delta_{t-m+1},\delta'_{t,m,t-m},\delta'_{t,m,t-m-1},\ldots),$$
